notes.short: Torn-out eyes: they would have given him anything
notes.about: Paul reminds the Galatians how much they once loved him: they would have torn out their eyes for him. The eyes are among the dearest parts of the body, and the saying means they would have given him anything, however dear.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.words: torn out your eyes and given them to me
figure.means: the greatest self-sacrifice: they would have given him anything, however dear

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among examples of Hyperbole. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a proverbial phrase for the greatest self-sacrifice, the eyes being among the dearest members. Clarke takes it as a proverbial expression for the strongest affection, and Barnes says they would have given him anything, however dear.
notes.limit: Some think the saying was chosen with a weakness in Paul's eyes in mind, as if they would have given him their own in place of his. The verses do not say what his illness was (Galatians 4:13-14).

cites.quote: Other examples of Hyperbole may be seen in 2Sa 17:13. ... Gal 4:15
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: ye would have plucked out your own eyes--one of the dearest members of the body--so highly did you value me: a proverbial phrase for the greatest self-sacrifice
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Dearer than one's eyes, or to profess to give one's eyes for the sake of a person, appears to have been a proverbial expression, intimating the highest tokens of the strongest affection.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: No higher proof of attachment could have been given. They loved him so much, that they would have given to him anything, however dear
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Paul's calling first and last, Peter's between
notes.about: Paul's calling to the uncircumcised comes first and last; Peter's calling to the circumcised is in the two middle lines.

lines.words: they saw that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised,
just as Peter had been to the circumcised.
For the One who was at work in Peter’s apostleship to the circumcised
was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles.

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets out these verses in four parts, Paul's commission in the first and last and Peter's in the two between. Boys gives the two parts he marks a to Paul's commission among the Gentiles, and speaks also of Peter's among the Jews.

cites.quote: In a. and a., St. Paul's commission to the Gentiles; … St. Peter's commission to the Jews.
cites.read: the 1824 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/tactica-sacra

cites.quote: a Paul’s commission. … b Peter’s. … b Peter’s. … a Paul’s commission.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Like a human covenant that no one can cancel
notes.about: Paul puts his point in human terms: once a human covenant is ratified, no one cancels it or adds to it. If that holds among men, God's covenant with Abraham holds all the more, so the law that came 430 years later cannot set aside the promise (verse 17).

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended
figure.means: God's covenant with Abraham: if no one sets aside a ratified human covenant, the law given later cannot set aside God's promise

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes: Paul draws an illustration from human dealings, and so it is with God's promise to Abraham. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): an illustration from everyday dealings; much less would God set aside His covenant. John Calvin: an argument from less to greater, by analogy from human bargains. W. Sanday (Ellicott): a figure from civil life that argues all the more for God.
notes.limit: Paul does not use the word like here: he reasons from a human covenant to God's, and in verse 17 he applies the picture.

cites.quote: I draw an illustration from what actually occurs among people. The illustration is, that when a contract or agreement is made by people involving obligations and promises, no one can add to it or take from it. It will remain as it was originally made. So with God. He made a solemn promise to Abraham.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: I take an illustration from a merely human transaction of everyday occurrence. ... no man disannulleth--"none setteth aside," not even the author himself, much less any second party. None does so who acts in common equity. Much less would the righteous God do so.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Though it be but a man’s covenant. This is an argument from the less to the greater. Human contracts are admitted on all hands to be binding: how much more what God has established? ... The analogy from which the apostle argues, would not apply so strictly to a testament as to a covenant. The apostle appears to reason from human bargains to that solemn covenant into which God entered with Abraham.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The figure that I am going to use is one taken from the ordinary civil relations between man and man, and therefore, it is left to be inferred, supplies an à fortiori argument in things relating to God, for men may change and break the most solemn engagements; God is absolutely faithful and unchangeable.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: The law pictured as a child’s guardian
notes.about: Paul pictures the law as a guardian: the household slave who watched over a boy and took him to school. Its charge was only for the years of childhood, and it led to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. Now that faith has come, believers are no longer under it.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.means: the law of Moses, which held God's people under its strict charge for a set time and pointed them to Christ

original.note: In Paul's Greek “guardian” is paidagōgos, the slave who had charge of a boy and took him to school and back; the English word pedagogue comes from it.

notes.evidence: John Calvin calls it Paul's second comparison: a schoolmaster serves only for childhood, and the law's authority was for a set age. Adam Clarke calls it a beautiful metaphor: the pedagogue was the servant who took children to school, as the law directed us to Christ. W. Sanday (Ellicott) explains the pedagogue slave, from whose name the English word comes, and calls it a metaphor.
notes.limit: One writer warns against pressing the metaphor so far as to make Christ the schoolmaster to whom the guardian brings the child.

cites.quote: This is the second comparison ... A schoolmaster is not appointed for the whole life, but only for childhood ... The comparison applies in both respects to the law, for its authority was limited to a particular age, and its whole object was to prepare its scholars in such a manner, that, when its elementary instructions were closed, they might make progress worthy of manhood.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The παιδαγωγος, pedagogue, is not the schoolmaster, but the servant who had the care of the children to lead them to and bring them back from school ... Thus the law did not teach us the living, saving knowledge; but, by its rites and ceremonies, and especially by its sacrifices, it directed us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. This is a beautiful metaphor
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Greek word is that from which is derived the English “pedagogue.” Originally it meant the slave who was placed in charge of a child, and whose duty it was to conduct it to school. ... They may be retained, provided that the metaphor is not pressed to the extent of supposing that Christ represents the schoolmaster proper to whom the child is led by the pedagogue slave.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A young heir kept under guardians for a time
notes.about: Paul likens God's people before Christ to a young heir. He owns everything, yet while a child he is no better off than a slave, kept under guardians and trustees until the date his father set. In the same way, Paul says, we were enslaved until the time God set, when He sent His Son (verses 3 and 4).

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: as long as the heir is a child, he is no different from a slave
figure.means: God's people before Christ came: heirs of the promise, yet kept under the law as a child under guardians until the time God set

notes.evidence: John Calvin calls it a third comparison, a minor under his tutor: the fathers of the Old Testament were sons, yet the law held them as a tutor until Christ came. Albert Barnes: Paul illustrates the state of a minor; the Jews before the Messiah were as an heir not yet of age. W. Sanday (Ellicott): the illustration holds in its chief points, the minor's constraint.
notes.limit: The picture is not pressed in every detail: one writer says it holds in its chief points, the constraint a minor lives under until he comes of age.

cites.quote: He does so by introducing a third comparison, drawn from the relation which a person under age bears to his tutor. ... the fathers under the Old Testament, being the sons of God, were free; but they were not in possession of freedom, while the law held the place of their tutor ... That slavery of the law lasted as long as it pleased God, who put an end to it at the coming of Christ.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This sentiment he proceeds further to illustrate by showing the true condition of one who was a minor. ... The idea which this is designed to illustrate is, that the condition of the Jews before the coming of the Messiah was inferior in many respects to what the condition of the friends of God would be under him - as inferior as the condition of an heir was before he was of age
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Both the child and the slave were subject to the same restraint, discipline, correction. ... The illustration does not hold good in all particulars, but in the chief particulars — viz., the state of constraint and subordination in which the minor is placed so long as he is a minor.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Paul reads a true history as a picture
notes.about: Paul says the account of Abraham's two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman, teaches more than it first tells: the two women stand for two covenants. Paul's own word names the figure, and the history remains true history.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.means: the true history of Hagar and Sarah and their sons, which Paul shows also sets forth the two covenants

original.note: In Paul's Greek the words are hatina estin allegoroumena, which things are allegorized; the verb is found nowhere else in the New Testament.

notes.evidence: Bullinger: a true history may be allegorized, shown to teach more, and remain true. Calvin: Paul does not mean Moses wrote it as an allegory, but finds in it a figurative picture of the two covenants that keeps the literal meaning. Barnes: it may be read allegorically without denying that the record is true. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): it has another besides the literal meaning.
notes.limit: The note does not claim that Moses wrote the account to be read this way, or that the events did not happen; Paul draws a further lesson from a true history.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 749
cites.quote: Gal 4:1-31 shows us that a true history may be allegorized (i.e., be shown to have further teaching in that which actually took place) without detracting from the truth of the history.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Paul certainly does not mean that Moses wrote the history for the purpose of being turned into an allegory, but points out in what way the history may be made to answer the present subject. ... but this does not involve a departure from the literal meaning. In a word, Paul adduces the history, as containing a figurative representation of the two covenants in the two wives of Abraham
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: May be regarded allegorically, or as illustrating great principles in regard to the condition of slaves and freemen ... He does not mean to say that the historical record of Moses was not true, or was merely allegorical ... The word does not occur elsewhere in the New Testament
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: are an allegory--rather, "are allegorical," that is, have another besides the literal meaning. these are the two covenants--"these [women] are (that is, mean; omit 'the' with all the oldest manuscripts) two covenants."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A common saying: a little leaven spreads
notes.about: Paul warns the Galatians with a saying he also uses in 1 Corinthians 5:6: a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough. What seems small will not stay small. Most read it of the church, where a few teachers or a little false teaching soon affects all; one reads it of a man's whole life.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough
figure.means: a little evil let in, such as a little false teaching or the few who bring it, which soon spreads through the whole

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes calls it evidently a proverbial expression and reads the leaven as a few false teachers whose teaching spread through the churches. Adam Clarke calls it a proverbial expression, aptly applied to the least tincture of false doctrine, which soon perverts the whole man. W. Sanday (Ellicott) calls it a proverb: the malcontents may be few, but they will soon ruin the whole church.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the leaven stands for: a little false teaching, or the few who brought it among the Galatians. One applies the saying to a single man, whose whole conduct a little false teaching soon perverts.

cites.quote: This is evidently a proverbial expression; see it explained in the notes at Co1 5:6 . ... the apostle means to say, that the influence which had brought this change about was at first small and unimportant; that there might have been but a few teachers of that kind ... but that the doctrines thus infused into the churches, had spread like leaven, until the whole mass had become affected.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A proverbial expression, see Co1 5:6 , very aptly applied to those who receive the smallest tincture of false doctrine, relative to the things essential to salvation, which soon influences the whole conduct, so that the man becomes totally perverted.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The proverb is true which says that a little leaven leavens the whole mass of dough. And so, in your case, the malcontents may be few, but they will soon ruin the whole Church. It seems decidedly more in accordance with the context to take the “little leaven” as referring rather to a few seceders than to a little bad doctrine.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Flesh against Spirit, and Spirit against flesh
notes.about: The flesh and the Spirit are named, then named again in reverse order: the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. The turn sets each against the other, and the verse then says so: “They are opposed to each other.”

figure.name: Antimetabole
figure.words: the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh
figure.means: the flesh and the Spirit, each set against the other

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Antimetabole, or Counterchange, words repeated in reverse order to oppose one thing to another, and sets it out: the flesh, against the spirit; and the spirit, against the flesh.
notes.limit: The note is about how the words are set out.

cites.quote: This figure repeats the word or words in a reverse order, for the purpose of opposing one thing to another, or of contrasting two or more things. ... a “ The flesh lusteth b against the spirit, b and the spirit a against the flesh. ”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: “Whatever a man sows, he will reap”
notes.about: Paul pictures a life as sowing and its end as harvest. What a man does is the seed, and he will reap a crop of the same kind: from sowing to please the flesh, destruction; from sowing to please the Spirit, eternal life.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return
figure.means: what a person does in this life is seed, and the harvest to come answers to it, ruin or eternal life

notes.evidence: John Calvin: Paul answers excuses for not giving with a comparison drawn from seed-time, the same metaphor as in 2 Corinthians. Albert Barnes: the figure is from farming; every grain yields its own kind, and so do our works. W. Sanday (Ellicott): the seed is a man's actions, sown in the field of the flesh or of the Spirit. Adam Clarke: to sow is a man's life here, to reap his lot hereafter.
notes.limit: Several of the writers tie the saying first to giving to those who teach the word (verse 6), then widen it to all a person does.

cites.quote: Paul meets these views by a comparison drawn from seed-time, which, he tells us, is a fit representation of acts of beneficence. On this subject we had occasion to speak, in expounding the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, where the same metaphor was employed.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This figure is taken from agriculture. A man who sows wheat, shall reap wheat; he who sows barley, shall reap barley; he who sows cockle, shall reap cockle. Every kind of grain will produce grain like itself. So it is in regard to our works. He who is liberal, shall be dealt with liberally; he who is righteous, shall be rewarded; he who is a sinner, shall reap according to his deeds.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The seed sown is a man’s actions here on earth. If the object of those actions is merely self-indulgence, they are, as it were, sown in a field the owner of which is the flesh ... where all the actions are like seed deposited in the field of which the owner and lord is the Spirit, that same Spirit will reward them in the world to come with the gift of everlasting life.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: In like manner, he that sows to the flesh - who indulges his sensual and animal appetites, shall have corruption as the crop ... To sow, here, means transacting the concerns of a man's natural life. To reap, signifies his enjoyment or punishment in another world.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)
